PullRequest.Title: mcp: handle HTTP stream cancellation during disposal
PullRequest.Body:
Stopping or disposing an HTTP MCP server can abort a pending SSE read. The reader is already errored, but the cleanup path called `reader.cancel()` and discarded the rejected promise, surfacing an unhandled `AbortError` during otherwise normal teardown.

- Skip redundant reader cancellation once disposal has already aborted the fetch.
- Await cancellation for active read failures, keeping cleanup in the handled promise chain and genuine failures visible.
- Add a disposal regression and an active-read-error control in the existing MCP host test suite.

Scenarios.Scenario: Send an MCP request whose HTTP response is an SSE stream and the response reader fails while the handle remains active
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Main-thread message IPC invokes ExtHostMcpService.$sendMessage; the handle performs the existing POST fetch, reads/parses the SSE response, publishes messages by IPC, and resolves send after the read loop ends. On a read failure, the changed await observes reader.cancel() before the existing warning path completes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dispatch the MCP request from the main thread to the extension host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One IPC call per outgoing MCP message
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same IPC dispatch occurred before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Starts request processing and is already on the send critical path

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: POST the MCP message and consume its response body
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One POST per message, plus response-body reads per delivered chunk
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same POST and stream reads occurred before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The fetch and response stream determine send completion

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish parsed MCP response messages or the stream warning to the main thread
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One receive-message IPC per parsed MCP message; at most one warning for this failed response
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same publication paths existed before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Message publication is required for response delivery; warning publication follows failure

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One response reader per in-flight POST request. The initial request is serialized while transport mode is unknown; after HTTP mode is established, sends can be concurrent, so failures scale with concurrently in-flight requests rather than SSE events or payload items.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: A Sequencer serializes only requests while mode is Unknown. Established HTTP requests can overlap without a shared limiter; each failed response independently reaches this catch once.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache participates. Authentication discovery/token behavior is unchanged, and neither warm nor cold state changes the stream cleanup branch.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: ReadableStream cancellation on an already errored stream returns a rejected promise with the stored error and does not execute the underlying source cancellation algorithm. Awaiting it adds promise observation but no network cancellation or input-scaling work.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Real deployments may vary in the number of simultaneous HTTP requests and stream failures, but the changed cancellation branch is reached only after the reader is already errored.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Before the diff cancellation was invoked without awaiting and the original read error was thrown; after the diff the same already-settled rejection is awaited. This handles the promise chain without adding a network boundary or multiplicative work.

Scenarios.Scenario: Dispose or stop an HTTP MCP handle while an SSE response read is pending
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Disposal marks the handle's DisposableStore disposed, aborts the shared fetch signal, and cancels the token. The pending read rejects; the changed disposed check returns before reader.cancel(), allowing teardown to complete without the redundant cancellation promise.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Request MCP server stop from the main thread
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One IPC call per server stop
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same stop IPC and close sequence occurred before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Initiates close; normal session close may complete before handle disposal

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Optionally send the existing HTTP DELETE session-close request
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one DELETE per HTTP MCP handle with a session ID
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same DELETE was awaited before disposal.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The stop path awaits this request before disposing the handle

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Abort active fetches/readers via the existing AbortController during disposal
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One shared abort signal per handle, affecting its active requests
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same abort occurred, followed by an unnecessary reader.cancel() call whose rejected promise was discarded.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Unblocks pending stream reads during teardown

Scenarios.ScalingInput: At most one backchannel reader plus the currently in-flight response readers per handle; cost scales with active requests at teardown, not message history.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: All active fetches share the handle AbortController and are aborted together. Each read loop independently observes disposal; no new work is scheduled by the diff.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: DisposableStore sets isDisposed before invoking registered abort/cancellation callbacks, so the changed catch branch returns before reader.cancel() for teardown-triggered failures.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of active response readers at disposal depends on concurrent requests, but the diff removes rather than adds a per-reader cleanup call on this path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No regression. The diff reduces redundant cleanup work and prevents a discarded rejected promise during disposal; it adds no retained resource or blocking boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: Maintain the streamable-HTTP GET backchannel across an active stream read failure
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The handle performs the existing GET, reads SSE notifications, reports the read failure, and re-enters the existing retry loop after its delay. The changed await occurs after the response stream is already errored and before the retry loop resumes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: GET and consume the MCP asynchronous-notification SSE backchannel
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One active GET per handle, repeated after failures according to the existing retry loop
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same GET, read loop, and reconnect schedule existed before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required for asynchronous notifications but off the outgoing message critical path

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish each backchannel MCP notification to the main thread
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One IPC call per parsed message event
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same event publication occurred before the diff.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One backchannel per HTTP MCP handle. Failures scale with reconnect attempts across active handles, with the existing retry delay capped at 30 seconds.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each handle has one sequential backchannel loop; multiple MCP handles may reconnect independently. The diff neither adds parallelism nor removes backoff.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No response cache is used. Session ID and Last-Event-ID are per-handle state and unchanged.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the stream is already errored when this catch executes, and the existing per-handle loop preserves its retry delay and single-stream concurrency.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Backchannel failure frequency and number of simultaneously configured servers vary, but cancellation remains constant-time promise observation per failed stream.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Awaiting the already-rejected cancellation promise does not add network cancellation, increase retry frequency, or fan out work.

Analysis.Summary: Reviewed the complete two-file diff and traced active response failures, handle disposal, and backchannel reconnects. The production change only changes error-promise handling after a stream read failure and removes redundant cancellation during disposal; no actionable performance regression or qualifying performance-regression fix was found.
